questions.stem: What is the default block size in Hadoop?
options: 4 MB
64 MB
128 MB
256 MB
1 GB
questions.explanation: Hadoop's default block size is 128 MB, although it can be changed.

questions.stem: How is HDFS best described in relation to Hadoop?
options: A Hadoop file system, comparable to FAT, NTFS or EXT
A query language for Hadoop tables
The Java framework that schedules Hadoop jobs
A wrapper that manages table structures
A compression codec for Hadoop blocks
questions.explanation: HDFS is the Hadoop file system, playing the same role that FAT, NTFS or EXT play on other systems.

questions.stem: What does Hive actually store when it presents data as tables?
options: A full copy of every HDFS file in its own database
Only the compressed version of each file
The data blocks but not the file names
A cached subset of frequently queried rows
No data at all; it only manages table structures on top of HDFS files
questions.explanation: Hive is only a wrapper: it behaves like tables in a traditional database but stores no data, managing table structures over files held in HDFS.

questions.stem: What are the two ways in which Hive can work with data?
options: Store data in memory or on tape
Store files in HDFS directly, or create tables which create HDFS files at the back end
Replicate files across nodes, or keep a single copy
Query files with SQL, or query them with MapReduce
Store data in HDFS, or store it in a relational database
questions.explanation: Hive either works over files stored directly in HDFS, or tables are created in Hive and the HDFS files are created at the back end.

questions.stem: If two 50 MB files are stored directly in HDFS, how many blocks are created?
options: None until a query is run
One shared block, because together they are under 128 MB
Four, because each file is split in half
Two, because each file stored in HDFS creates its own block
One block per node in the cluster
questions.explanation: Each file stored directly in HDFS creates its own block, so two 50 MB files produce two blocks.

questions.stem: If the same two 50 MB files are loaded through Hive tables instead of directly into HDFS, how are they stored?
options: In two separate blocks, exactly as with direct HDFS storage
Both in a single block, because Hive manages its own blocks
In a Hive-owned database outside HDFS
In one block per column
They are rejected because they are smaller than 128 MB
questions.explanation: Hive manages its own blocks, so two small 50 MB files can be stored together in a single block.

questions.stem: Why do thousands of 1 MB files arriving from social media cause a problem when stored directly in HDFS?
options: Each creates its own small block, and thousands of small blocks hurt MPP performance
HDFS cannot store files smaller than the block size
Hive refuses to build tables over files that small
Small files cannot be replicated
They exceed the cluster's total block count
questions.explanation: Every small file becomes its own small block, and thousands of tiny blocks degrade massive parallel processing performance.

questions.stem: What block size is described as best practice for Hadoop?
options: 1 MB
50 MB
64 MB
100 MB
128 MB
questions.explanation: The best practice is to have blocks of 128 MB, avoiding the performance cost of many small blocks.

questions.stem: Which kinds of data can Hadoop's open-source framework store?
options: Structured data only
Unstructured data only
Semi-structured and unstructured data, but not structured
Structured, semi-structured and unstructured data
Only data that has first been converted to CSV
questions.explanation: Hadoop is an open-source framework to store structured, semi-structured and unstructured data.

questions.stem: Which statement about Hive is NOT correct?
options: Hive behaves like tables in a traditional database
Hive is a wrapper on top of files stored in HDFS
Hive keeps its own separate copy of the data apart from HDFS
Hive can create HDFS files at the back end when tables are created
Hive manages its own blocks
questions.explanation: Hive does not store any data of its own; it manages table structures over files that live in HDFS.
